sections.h: 1 Maccabees: a high priesthood outside Zadok's line, and the Wicked Priest
sections.b:
The Zadokite high priests lost the office in the crisis of the 170s BC: Onias III was deposed and killed (2 Maccabees 4:7–34), and his son Onias IV fled to Egypt, where Ptolemy VI let him build a temple at Leontopolis (Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73). The kings then gave or sold the office to Jason, Menelaus and Alcimus. After Alcimus died in 159 BC, 1 Maccabees names no high priest until King Alexander Balas appoints Jonathan in 152 BC (1 Maccabees 9:56; 1 Maccabees 10:20–21). Jonathan's family belonged to the priestly course of Joarib (1 Maccabees 2:1; 1 Chronicles 24:7), but not to Zadok's house. 1 Maccabees tells the appointment without apology, and its account of Simon's election "until a faithful prophet arises" (1 Maccabees 14:41) reads like a defense of a line with no claim by birth.

The Wicked Priest. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran speaks of a "Wicked Priest" who "was called by the name of truth when he first arose" but grew proud, abandoned God for wealth, and persecuted the community's "Teacher of Righteousness" (1QpHab 8:8–13; 11:4–8), and was finally handed over to his enemies (1QpHab 9:9–12). Since the 1950s many scholars, among them Geza Vermes, J. T. Milik, Hartmut Stegemann and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, have identified him with Jonathan: a priest welcomed at first, who took the office from a pagan king and died a prisoner of Tryphon (1 Maccabees 13:23). Stegemann went further, suggesting the Teacher had served as high priest in the years after Alcimus, and was pushed out when Jonathan took the robe. Frank Moore Cross preferred Simon, who was murdered with his sons at a banquet near Jericho (1 Maccabees 16:11–16). The Groningen hypothesis of Florentino García Martínez and Adam van der Woude reads the title as a series of Hasmonean high priests, one after another. Others point to later rulers such as Alexander Jannaeus. The texts give no names, and many scholars now treat any single identification as uncertain.

common: Many scholars identify the Qumran "Wicked Priest" with Jonathan, the first Hasmonean high priest (1 Maccabees 10:21).
uncommon: Hartmut Stegemann proposed that the Teacher of Righteousness was the high priest in the years after Alcimus died (1 Maccabees 9:56), and was displaced when Jonathan was appointed.

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: a high priest appointed by a king
sections.b: Jonathan becomes high priest by a letter of Alexander Balas, who sends him the purple and a gold crown with it, and he first wears "the holy robe" at the Feast of Booths in 152 BC (1 Maccabees 10:18–21). Each later king confirms him: Demetrius II (1 Maccabees 11:27) and Antiochus VI (1 Maccabees 11:57). The same man is general, governor and royal Friend (1 Maccabees 10:65). The joining of the priesthood with army command, and later with kingship, marks the Hasmonean state. Critics within Judaism objected: the Pharisees asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood, according to Josephus (Antiquities 13.288–292), and some Dead Sea Scrolls attack a "Wicked Priest" (see Zadok). Hebrews 5:4 states the older ideal, that no one takes the honor of the high priesthood for himself unless God calls him, as he called Aaron.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 10:18–21; 1 Maccabees 10:65; 1 Maccabees 11:27; 1 Maccabees 11:57; Hebrews 5:4; Numbers 25:10–13

sections.b: When Judas falls at Elasa, his brothers bury him at Modein and "all Israel" mourns him with the words "How the warrior has fallen, the one who saved Israel!" (1 Maccabees 9:20–21). The cry borrows David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, "How the warriors have fallen!" (2 Samuel 1:19; 2 Samuel 1:25; 2 Samuel 1:27), and the judges' role as rescuers, as when the LORD raised up "a rescuer" for Israel (Judges 3:9). The next verse borrows the closing formula of the books of Kings (1 Maccabees 9:22; 1 Kings 11:41). Elsewhere in the same chapter a wedding is turned into mourning and music into lament (1 Maccabees 9:41), as in Amos 8:10.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 9:19–22; 1 Maccabees 9:41; 2 Samuel 1:19–27; Judges 3:9; 1 Kings 11:41; Amos 8:10

sections.h: The second Jonathan at Michmash (1 Maccabees 9)
sections.b: After the death of Judas, his brother Jonathan led the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 9:28–31). When the fighting ended in about 157 BC, he "settled at Michmash" and "began to judge the people" (1 Maccabees 9:73), at the place where Jonathan son of Saul had routed the Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 13:23; 1 Samuel 14:1–14). The writer has just echoed David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (1 Maccabees 9:21), so the second Jonathan's base at Michmash is likely meant to be heard as an echo of the first. Both Jonathans died at the hands of foreign enemies (1 Samuel 31:2; 1 Maccabees 13:23).
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 9:28–31; 1 Maccabees 9:73; 1 Maccabees 13:23; 1 Samuel 13:23; 1 Samuel 14:1–14; 1 Samuel 31:2

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Jonathan burns the temple of Dagon
sections.b: Dagon's temple at Ashdod (Greek Azotus) still stood in the 140s BC. After the battle of 147 BC, the beaten cavalry fled into "Beth-dagon, the temple of their idol", and Jonathan burned it with the people inside (1 Maccabees 10:83–85). When Ptolemy VI passed by, the people of Azotus showed him the ruins (1 Maccabees 11:4). For a reader who knew 1 Samuel 5, where Dagon's statue fell face down before the ark, the burning finished the old story.

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Jonathan's battle in the plain of Hazor
sections.b: In about 144 BC Jonathan camped by the Sea of Galilee and marched to "the plain of Hazor" to meet the generals of Demetrius II, who had come to Kedesh (1 Maccabees 11:63–74). Alexandrinus reads "Nasor", but Sinaiticus and Josephus (Antiquities 13.158) have Hazor. Ambushed, his army fled; Jonathan tore his clothes, put dust on his head and prayed, then turned the battle. Joshua had fought the kings of the north at Hazor (Joshua 11:1–11), and Barak of Kedesh fought Jabin of Hazor (Judges 4:2–6).

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Judas and Jonathan as new judges
sections.b: 1 Maccabees tells the brothers' story in the language of Judges. Judas is mourned as the one "who saved Israel" (1 Maccabees 9:21), as the judges were raised to rescue it (Judges 3:9). After Alcimus dies, "the land of Judah was quiet for two years" (1 Maccabees 9:57), and after Bacchides leaves, "the sword came to rest in Israel" and Jonathan "began to judge the people" (1 Maccabees 9:73), as Judges closes each episode: "So the land was quiet for forty years" (Judges 3:11; compare Judges 3:30; Judges 8:28). Like the judges, Jonathan rules without royal title, until the kings give him one.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 9:21; 1 Maccabees 9:57; 1 Maccabees 9:73; Judges 2:16–18; Judges 3:9–11; Judges 3:30; Judges 8:28; 1 Samuel 7:15–17

sections.b: 1 Maccabees describes the distress after Judas's death as the worst "since the day a prophet was last seen among them" (1 Maccabees 9:27). The book twice more looks for a future prophet: the stones of the defiled altar are stored "until a prophet should come" (1 Maccabees 4:46), and Simon is made leader "until a faithful prophet arises" (1 Maccabees 14:41). Psalm 74:9 had already lamented, "There is no prophet now." Josephus (Against Apion 1.41) and the rabbis (Tosefta Sotah 13:3) also speak of prophecy as ended after the Persian period. Christian readers have connected the waiting to the prophet promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18 and to John the Baptist (John 1:21). Whether prophecy continues in the church is carded at Numbers 11.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 4:46; 1 Maccabees 9:27; 1 Maccabees 14:41; Psalm 74:9; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; John 1:21

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Jonathan's first service as high priest
sections.b: Jonathan first put on the high priest's robe "in the seventh month of the year 160, at the Feast of Booths", in October 152 BC (1 Maccabees 10:21). The pilgrim crowds of the feast made it the most public moment of the year. 2 Maccabees links the first Hanukkah to Booths as well (2 Maccabees 10:6).

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: three districts taken from Samaria
sections.b: In the bidding war of the 150s and 140s BC, Demetrius I promised and Demetrius II granted that three districts, Aphairema, Lydda and Rathamin, be moved from Samaria to Judea (1 Maccabees 10:30; 1 Maccabees 10:38; 1 Maccabees 11:28; 1 Maccabees 11:34). The grant is "for all who sacrifice in Jerusalem" (1 Maccabees 11:34), a definition that leaves out those who worshiped at Gerizim. Antiochus VI speaks of four districts (1 Maccabees 11:57). The Samaritan temple itself was laid waste when John Hyrcanus took Gerizim later in the century (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255–256).
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 10:30; 1 Maccabees 10:38; 1 Maccabees 11:28; 1 Maccabees 11:34; 1 Maccabees 11:57; John 4:20

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Azotus, Ascalon, Ekron and Gaza
sections.b: The old Philistine cities were Greek cities by the 100s BC, but 1 Maccabees still calls their troops "foreigners" (ἀλλόφυλοι), the Greek Old Testament's word for Philistines (1 Maccabees 11:68; 1 Maccabees 11:74). Jonathan burns Azotus (Ashdod) and its temple of Dagon (1 Maccabees 10:84), is welcomed at Ascalon (1 Maccabees 10:86; 1 Maccabees 11:60), receives Ekron from Alexander Balas (1 Maccabees 10:89) and takes hostages from Gaza (1 Maccabees 11:61–62). The prophets had foretold judgment on these cities (Zephaniah 2:4; Zechariah 9:5–7).
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 10:84–89; 1 Maccabees 11:4; 1 Maccabees 11:60–62; 1 Maccabees 11:68; Zephaniah 2:4; Zechariah 9:5–7

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Ptolemy VI and the Seleucid throne
sections.b: Ptolemy VI Philometor married his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander Balas at Ptolemais in 150 BC (1 Maccabees 10:51–58), then took her back, gave her to Demetrius II and entered Antioch (1 Maccabees 11:1–13). He beat Alexander in battle but died of his wounds days later, in 145 BC (1 Maccabees 11:15–18). 1 Maccabees says he came "by trickery" (1 Maccabees 11:1); Josephus and Diodorus give a kinder account. The same king had let the exiled high priest Onias IV build a temple at Leontopolis in Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73).

Judas died at Elasa in spring 160 BC (1 Maccabees 9:1–18), and for a time the renegades ruled Judea with Bacchides' help (1 Maccabees 9:23–27). Jonathan led the survivors in the desert (1 Maccabees 9:33–49), until a truce in about 157 BC left him the real ruler of the countryside (1 Maccabees 9:70–73). From 152 BC the rival Seleucid kings bid for his support, and he won by diplomacy what Judas had not won by war: the high priesthood, royal titles, tax relief and new territory (1 Maccabees 10:1–11:59). The revolt for the law had become a small state.

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: the Temple as a place of asylum
sections.b: Demetrius I offered that anyone who fled to the Temple in Jerusalem, or within its bounds, for a debt to the king "or for any other matter" should be released (1 Maccabees 10:43). The right of asylum was common for Greek temples. The Torah's asylum was narrower, for those who had killed by accident (Exodus 21:13–14; Numbers 35:9–15). Kedesh in Galilee, an old city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), is the base of Demetrius II's generals in 1 Maccabees 11:63.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 10:43; 1 Maccabees 11:63; Exodus 21:13–14; Numbers 35:9–15; Joshua 20:7; 1 Kings 1:50–53

sections.h: 1 Maccabees: Mount Zion as the Temple hill
sections.b: In 1 Maccabees "Mount Zion" means the Temple mount, set over against the Citadel in "the city of David" (1 Maccabees 4:37; 1 Maccabees 4:60). Jonathan, settled in Jerusalem, had the walls rebuilt and Mount Zion ringed with squared stones (1 Maccabees 10:10–11), so that the Citadel's garrison could not again reach the sanctuary.

sections.h: Jonathan: from desert leader to the king's Kinsman (1 Maccabees 9–11)
sections.b: After Judas died in 160 BC, his brother Jonathan led the movement from the wilderness of Tekoa (1 Maccabees 9:28–49), made a truce with Bacchides, and ruled from Michmash (1 Maccabees 9:70–73). When Alexander Balas challenged Demetrius I in 152 BC, both kings bid for him. Alexander made him high priest and Friend of the King, with purple and a gold crown (1 Maccabees 10:18–21), then First Friend, general and governor (1 Maccabees 10:65), and gave him the gold brooch of the Kinsmen and the city of Ekron (1 Maccabees 10:89). Demetrius II and Antiochus VI confirmed and enlarged these grants, and Simon was made governor of the coast (1 Maccabees 11:27; 1 Maccabees 11:57–59). His troops rescued Demetrius II in Antioch (1 Maccabees 11:44–51). For the debate whether the Dead Sea Scrolls' "Wicked Priest" is Jonathan, see Zadok.
sections.refs: 1 Maccabees 9:28–73; 1 Maccabees 10:18–21; 1 Maccabees 10:59–66; 1 Maccabees 10:89; 1 Maccabees 11:20–37; 1 Maccabees 11:44–51; 1 Maccabees 11:57–59

sections.b: Alexander Balas, who claimed to be a son of Antiochus IV, landed at Ptolemais in 152 BC with backing from Rome, Pergamum and Egypt (1 Maccabees 10:1; Polybius 33.18). He defeated and killed Demetrius I in 150 BC (1 Maccabees 10:48–50) and married Cleopatra Thea, daughter of Ptolemy VI (1 Maccabees 10:57–58). In 147 BC Demetrius II landed with Cretan mercenaries (1 Maccabees 10:67). Ptolemy turned against Alexander, who was beaten and killed in 145 BC; Ptolemy died days later (1 Maccabees 11:8–18). Demetrius II dismissed his father's troops and lost their loyalty (1 Maccabees 11:38), and his former officer Tryphon crowned Alexander's young son as Antiochus VI and took Antioch (1 Maccabees 11:39–40; 1 Maccabees 11:54–56). Each claimant needed the Jewish army, and the Hasmoneans gained from every change of king.

sections.h: 1 Maccabees 10–11: playing one king against another
sections.b: In chapters 10–11 Jonathan's alliances are with Seleucid kings, not Rome. Demetrius I offers him the right to raise an army (1 Maccabees 10:6); Alexander outbids him with the high priesthood (1 Maccabees 10:20); Demetrius answers with sweeping tax relief and a gift of Ptolemais (1 Maccabees 10:25–45). The people "did not trust" Demetrius, remembering his past (1 Maccabees 10:46), and the book shows royal promises failing: Demetrius II "proved false in everything he had said" (1 Maccabees 11:53), and Jonathan went over to Antiochus VI (1 Maccabees 11:57). Psalm 146:3 had warned, "Do not rely on nobles."
